Planning a Bicycle Route Across the City

A daily bicycle route is a small engineering problem. The shortest line on the map is rarely the fastest line in traffic. A rider weighs surface quality, the number of stops, the slope of every street and the chance of a flat tyre. A calm street with one hill beats a fast road with four junctions.

What to measure first

Start with the distance and the time you can spend. Then check the surface: asphalt, gravel or paving stones. Paving stones are slower and they shake the frame. Next, count the traffic lights and the left turns across two lanes. Each left turn costs more time than a hill.

  • Distance and riding time
  • Surface of every street
  • Junctions and left turns
  • Hills on the way

A spare plan

Weather changes the plan more often than traffic. A rider needs one dry route and one wet route. The wet route uses wider streets and avoids gravel. A repair kit, a pump and a spare tube belong to the bag, not to the shelf at home.
